questions.question_text: The main weakness of the Articles of Confederation that Shays' Rebellion exposed was:
questions.option_b: The national government's inability to raise an army or enforce laws
questions.explanation: Under the Articles, Congress couldn't tax directly or compel states to fund a response to the uprising — the impotence that pushed elites toward the Constitutional Convention. There WAS no executive to be overly powerful; that's the reverse trap.

questions.question_text: Federalist No. 10 argues that a large republic best controls the dangers of faction because:
questions.option_a: Factions can be banned in large republics
questions.option_b: A multiplicity of interests makes it harder for any single faction to form a tyrannical majority
questions.option_c: Large republics eliminate the causes of faction
questions.explanation: Madison says the CAUSES of faction are 'sown in the nature of man' — you can't remove them without destroying liberty; you can only control EFFECTS. Extend the sphere and no single interest dominates. Required-document question, asked nearly every year.

questions.question_text: Brutus No. 1 would most likely object to which modern development?
questions.option_b: The expansive use of the Necessary and Proper Clause to justify broad federal programs
questions.explanation: Brutus warned that the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses would let the national government swallow the states — exactly the anti-federalist fear of consolidated power over a large republic. Pairing Brutus 1 against Federalist 10 is the classic SAQ matchup.

questions.question_text: Categorical grants differ from block grants in that categorical grants:
questions.option_a: Give states broad discretion over spending
questions.option_b: Come with specific conditions and federal strings attached
questions.explanation: Categorical = narrow purpose + conditions (how Washington steers states); block = broad purpose + state discretion (states' preference). Which grant type expands FEDERAL influence is the actual point being tested.

questions.question_text: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) established which two principles?
questions.option_b: Implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and federal supremacy over state taxation
questions.option_d: Commerce power limits and state sovereignty
questions.explanation: Marshall upheld the national bank via implied powers ('let the end be legitimate...') and voided Maryland's tax ('the power to tax involves the power to destroy'). Judicial review is Marbury — swapping the two landmark Marshall cases is the standard distractor.

questions.question_text: Which power belongs exclusively to the Senate?
questions.option_b: Confirming federal judges and ratifying treaties
questions.option_d: Choosing the president when the Electoral College deadlocks
questions.explanation: Advice and consent — confirmations and treaties (2/3) — is the Senate's alone. Revenue bills START in the House; the House impeaches (indicts) while the Senate tries; the House picks the president in a deadlock. Each chamber's exclusive list is guaranteed exam content.

questions.question_text: A senator speaks for eleven hours to delay a vote on a bill. Ending this tactic requires:
questions.option_b: A cloture vote of 60 senators
questions.option_d: A ruling by the Chief Justice
questions.explanation: The filibuster exploits the Senate's unlimited-debate tradition; cloture (Rule XXII) needs 60 votes. The practical effect: most major legislation needs a 60-vote supermajority — a structural reason for gridlock the FRQs love.

questions.question_text: Drawing district lines to dilute the opposing party's votes by packing them into few districts or cracking them across many is called:
questions.option_b: Partisan gerrymandering
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering is the MANIPULATION; redistricting is the neutral process; reapportionment reallocates seats among states after the census. Baker v. Carr made districting justiciable ('one person, one vote') — connect the vocabulary to the required case.

questions.question_text: Presidents increasingly rely on executive orders and executive agreements rather than legislation and treaties because:
questions.option_b: They bypass congressional approval, though they are easier for successors to reverse
questions.option_d: The Supreme Court mandates the practice
questions.explanation: Unilateral tools avoid gridlock but rest on shakier ground — the next president can undo them with a signature. Speed versus durability is the trade-off the exam wants articulated; 'permanent once signed' is the exact opposite of the truth.

questions.question_text: Congress can override a presidential veto with:
questions.option_a: A simple majority in both chambers
questions.option_b: A two-thirds vote in both chambers
questions.option_c: A three-fourths vote in the Senate alone
questions.explanation: 2/3 of BOTH chambers — deliberately difficult (overrides succeed under 5% of the time), making the veto threat itself a powerful bargaining chip. Three-fourths belongs to constitutional amendment ratification, a different supermajority.

questions.question_text: Marbury v. Madison (1803) is foundational because it established:
questions.option_b: Judicial review — the courts' power to strike down laws conflicting with the Constitution
questions.explanation: Marshall declared 'it is emphatically the province... of the judicial department to say what the law is' — a power found nowhere explicit in Article III. The irony: the Court built its strongest weapon while declining to act in the case at hand.

questions.question_text: A justice who believes the Court should generally defer to elected branches and avoid striking down laws practices:
questions.option_b: Judicial restraint
questions.explanation: Restraint = deference to democratic majorities; activism = willingness to overturn them. Note neither maps cleanly onto liberal/conservative — striking down a progressive law is also activism. Stare decisis (following precedent) is a separate axis entirely.

questions.question_text: Through which mechanism have most Bill of Rights protections been applied to the states?
questions.option_b: Selective incorporation via the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights originally bound only the federal government; the Court has incorporated rights against states case by case through 14th Amendment due process — e.g., McDonald v. Chicago (2nd Amendment, 2010). 'Selective' = one right at a time, not wholesale.

questions.question_text: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) held that students wearing black armbands to protest the Vietnam War were protected because:
questions.option_a: Schools are private actors not bound by the First Amendment
questions.option_b: Symbolic speech is protected unless it substantially disrupts the educational environment
questions.option_c: All student speech is unprotected at school
questions.explanation: 'Students don't shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate' — armbands were silent, passive, non-disruptive symbolic speech. The substantial-disruption test is the standard; later cases (Hazelwood, Morse) carve exceptions, which is the comparison FRQs exploit.

questions.question_text: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned which precedent?
questions.option_a: Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine
questions.option_b: Marbury v. Madison
questions.explanation: Brown held that separate educational facilities are 'inherently unequal,' demolishing Plessy's 1896 doctrine under the Equal Protection Clause. Know the pairing: Plessy builds the wall, Brown tears it down — and Brown's enforcement required executive action (Little Rock, 1957).

questions.question_text: Compared with general elections, voters in primary elections tend to be:
questions.option_b: More ideologically extreme and more politically engaged
questions.explanation: Low-turnout primaries attract the most committed partisans — pushing candidates toward the wings in primaries, then back to the center for the general (the 'pivot'). This dynamic is a stock explanation for polarization in FRQ answers.

questions.question_text: Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held that:
questions.option_a: Corporations may donate unlimited sums directly to candidates
questions.option_b: Independent political expenditures by corporations and unions are protected speech that cannot be capped
questions.explanation: The ruling protects INDEPENDENT expenditures (not coordinated with campaigns) as speech — enabling super PACs. Direct corporate contributions to candidates remain banned, and individual contribution limits still exist. The independent/direct distinction is where every distractor lives.

questions.question_text: Which factor is the strongest predictor of whether an individual will vote?
questions.option_b: Educational attainment
questions.explanation: Education tops every participation model — it builds civic skills, political efficacy, and registration know-how, and it correlates with age and income, the other big predictors. Demographics explain turnout patterns far better than geography.

questions.question_text: The 'iron triangle' describes the mutually beneficial relationship among:
questions.option_a: The president, Congress, and the courts
questions.option_b: A bureaucratic agency, a congressional committee, and an interest group
questions.option_d: The two major parties and the media
questions.explanation: Agencies get budgets, committees get electoral support, interest groups get favorable policy — a closed, self-reinforcing loop (e.g., Pentagon–Armed Services Committees–defense contractors). Option A is checks and balances, the opposite of cozy cooperation.

questions.question_text: Mandatory spending such as Social Security and Medicare constrains fiscal policymaking because:
questions.option_b: It grows automatically by formula, leaving a shrinking share of the budget for discretionary choices
questions.option_c: It is set by the Federal Reserve
questions.explanation: Entitlements pay out by eligibility formula without yearly votes — now roughly two-thirds of federal spending — so Congress fights over an ever-thinner discretionary slice. 'Reauthorized annually' describes discretionary appropriations, the reverse of mandatory.
